title: Demystifying Action Space Design for Robotic Manipulation
one_liner: Changing how a robot describes its movements—whether it says absolute positions or relative nudges—dramatically shapes how easily it learns from demonstrations.
lead: Teaching a robot to manipulate objects by watching humans do it seems straightforward: collect videos, train a model, done. But how you let the model describe its moves—whether it outputs absolute hand positions or relative nudges—fundamentally changes what the model learns and how well it controls. This paper tests 500+ trained models on real robots to uncover which choices actually work and why.

problem.h2: How does a robot even describe what it is doing?
paras: When you teach a robot to pick up a cup by showing it videos of a human doing it, the robot learns a deep neural network—a mathematical model with thousands of numbers. That model ingests an image and outputs a command: how the robot's arm should move. But what should that command be? Should it say 'move the hand to a specific spot in space, like the coordinates for the cup'? Or 'nudge the hand 2 centimeters forward and 1 centimeter left from where it is right now'? Both describe motion, but they ask the model to solve different problems.

Today, engineers pick this choice by gut feeling or copy old projects. A beginner trying the wrong choice builds a robot that flails, fails to grasp objects, or works so badly nobody bothers tuning it. The problem is nobody had measured which choice actually matters or why.

callout.html: This paper tests whether robots learn faster when they predict absolute hand positions or relative nudges—the choice matters because delta actions create simpler training problems, so models find good solutions faster.

steps.text: Choose whether the model outputs absolute position or relative nudge.
Record 13,000+ robot demonstrations from human operators.
Train separate models with each action choice on the same data.
Run each trained model on four manipulation tasks to measure learning success.
Compare stability, learning speed, and task success across all designs.

paras: The robot's action space—the vocabulary it uses to describe its own moves. Instead of letting each robot project choose arbitrarily, the paper tests two core designs: whether the model predicts absolute hand coordinates in the world, or relative displacements from the hand's current position.

hidden.h2: Learnability: how quickly the model figures out the task
hidden.name: task convergence speed
paras: Learnability is the simplest question: given a fixed amount of training data (say, 100 human demonstrations), how many training steps does the model need before it consistently grasps the cup? A model trained on delta actions tends to converge in fewer steps than one trained on absolute positions, because predicting small nudges is a simpler problem mathematically. The paper measures this by counting how many gradient updates (adjustments to the model's weights) are needed to reach 80% success on held-out test rollouts.

The paper estimates this by training each model variant and recording at what training step performance plateaued. Faster convergence means the model learned the task's core structure earlier, because when a model reaches 80% success in fewer steps, it has found the essential relationship between images and movements more efficiently.

heat.caption: Darker means faster convergence. Delta actions and joint-space converge most reliably.

reads.html: How many training iterations until the robot stops improving and reaches its final performance on new test scenarios.
The paper plots learning curves (success rate vs. training step) for each model variant and measures the step at which the curve flattens to within 5% of final performance.

mechanism.h2: Why delta actions work better: the math of small changes
paras: Imagine the robot's hand is currently at position (0.5, 0.3, 0.8) in 3D space. If the model must predict the absolute target position, it must learn to output a specific coordinate. But that coordinate changes depending on where the hand started. In one demo the hand started at (0.4, 0.25, 0.75), in another at (0.6, 0.35, 0.85). The model sees different starting positions and must predict different targets—the relationship between input and output is entangled with irrelevant details like where the hand happens to begin.

Delta actions cut through this. Instead of learning absolute positions, the model learns nudges: 'forward 0.1 meters, left 0.05 meters'. These nudges are the same regardless of starting position. The model learns a simpler, more generalizable rule. The error surfaces become simpler and smoother—fewer jittery directions, fewer ways for gradient descent (the process that tunes the model's weights) to get stuck in local dead-ends. A simpler error surface means fewer training steps to find good weights.

Joint-space vs. task-space is orthogonal. Joint-space means predicting how much each motor should rotate; task-space means predicting hand position or pose in Cartesian coordinates. Joint-space is closer to the hardware physics, so small errors in the model's predictions translate directly to small errors in the actual motion—the system is stable because the hardware naturally dampens noise. Task-space actions are more intuitive to learn from (humans naturally demonstrate in hand-space), so the model generalizes to new scenarios better, because the relationship between image and hand position is simpler than the relationship between image and motor angles, which depends on the arm's current pose. The paper finds both matter, in different ways.

stages.s: Model learns the nudge, not the target
Same nudge applies whether hand started high or low
Same pattern across all starting positions, less to memorize

math.words: The model outputs a movement command. With absolute actions, that is a 3D target position. With delta actions, it is a 3D displacement. The loss—the error the model tries to minimize—is the squared distance between the predicted move and the observed human move.

charts.title: Absolute action baseline
charts.note: The model takes many steps to learn the mapping from starting position to target.

charts.title: Delta action (this paper)
charts.note: The model learns faster with nudges because the correct answer (move forward 0.1) stays the same across all starting positions, so each training example consistently teaches the same lesson, and the weights land in the right place sooner.

items.b: Stacking errors: predicting one nudge at a time can drift.
items.html: If the model makes a small mistake in the first nudge, the hand ends up slightly off. The next prediction assumes the hand is in the right spot, leading to cascading error. This matters over long trajectories (many steps). Absolute actions are immune because each command specifies the exact target, not relative to the previous position.

items.b: Joint-space actions work only with known kinematics.
items.html: Predicting motor rotations assumes the exact robot hardware is known (arm length, joint limits). If the hardware varies slightly between units or degrades over time, the action fails. Task-space avoids this by working in hand coordinates, not motor space.

Predicting hand position in 3D space works well on new scenarios with the same arm, but if the task involves rotating the wrist or precise orientation, hand position alone is not enough. A task-space action should include rotation or orientation to handle complex manipulation.

items.b: Done right: use delta task-space actions for speed, joint-space for stability.
items.html: The paper shows delta + task-space learns fastest and generalizes. For tasks requiring tight control, add a joint-space stabilizing layer on top.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulated robot arm (using a physics simulator like PyBullet). Collect 50 human demonstrations of reaching for an object. Train two models on the same data: one predicting absolute hand positions, one predicting delta movements. Record training loss and test success rate (does the robot reach the object?) over 500 training steps. Plot both curves on the same graph.
demo.metric_eq: convergence_speed = step at which success >= 80% for the first time
demo.closing: The delta model should reach 80% success in roughly half the training steps compared to absolute positions, even though both see the same demonstrations and start from random weights.
